weight-loss-jabs-glp-1-for-face-leaning.text: Users take GLP-1 jabs such as semaglutide to lose weight and, with it, facial fat, aiming for a leaner, more defined face. The facial hollowing sometimes called "Ozempic face" is debated. The medicines are studied for weight loss; their effect on facial appearance specifically is based mostly on anecdote and case discussion.

peptide-stacks-wolverine-stack.text: Forum users pair BPC-157 with TB-500 (the "Wolverine stack") to speed recovery from injuries and training so they can keep lifting for physique gains. Broader peptide stacks are also discussed for skin, bone mass or height. Support comes from animal data and anecdote, with no human trials on appearance outcomes.

anti-estrogen-ai-for-masculine-look.text: Aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole are used off-label to lower oestrogen for a leaner, more masculine look, less water retention and less breast tissue, and by younger users in pursuit of extra height. They are approved for other medical uses; trials in healthy men for these appearance goals are lacking.

minoxidil-finasteride-stack.text: Known as "fin+min", this pairing is the baseline regimen in looksmaxxing communities for keeping or thickening scalp hair in male pattern hair loss. Both drugs are approved for this use individually and backed by trials; the combination is discussed on forums as the standard starting point.

chain: Thicker scalp, brow and beard hair
oral-minoxidil.text: Users take low-dose oral minoxidil as a convenient alternative to topical minoxidil for scalp hair, and also discuss it for eyebrows, beard and lashes. It is used off-label by dermatologists for hair loss, with trials in that area; the facial hair use rests mostly on anecdote and case reports.

chain: Hair loss slows, density may improve
dutasteride-mesotherapy.text: Clinicians inject dilute dutasteride into the scalp as an off-label hair-loss treatment, discussed in hair communities as an alternative to oral dutasteride or finasteride. Evidence consists of small early trials and a growing set of case reports.

jelqing.text: Practitioners use jelqing, a manual stroking technique, in the belief that it enlarges the penis through stretching and tissue remodelling. The idea comes from anecdote and traditional claims; no published clinical studies have measured an enlargement effect.

hair-oiling.text: A long-standing South Asian practice, hair oiling uses coconut oil or herbal blends on hair and scalp for shine, softness and scalp care. In looksmaxxing circles it is also discussed for growth and slowing graying. Lab data and surveys exist; trials for growth or graying are lacking.

nofap-semen-retention.text: Followers of NoFap and semen retention abstain in the belief that it raises testosterone, confidence and attractiveness. The testosterone claim traces to a 2003 study that was later retracted; the looks and confidence benefits themselves have not been shown in studies.

carnivore-diet.text: People eating only animal foods describe clearer skin, a leaner body and a more defined jaw as benefits. Some also credit it with higher testosterone and strength. Human evidence for these appearance outcomes is sparse and rests mainly on testimonials.

chain: More growth, better skin and bones
raw-meat-raw-liver-diet.text: Some forum members eat raw meat, organs and dairy expecting more natural IGF-1 and growth hormone, better skin and stronger development. The expected benefits come from anecdote and theory; no human trials have tested the diet for appearance outcomes.

chain: Claimed growth, skin and digestion gains
raw-milk.text: In primal and carnivore-style circles raw milk is discussed for height in adolescents, skin, digestion and hormones. Reviews of nutrient content find little difference from pasteurized milk, and the appearance claims rest on anecdote.

seed-oil-avoidance.text: Followers exclude canola, soybean, sunflower and similar oils in the belief they drive inflammation that shows up as skin problems, puffiness and body fat. It is bundled with other clean-eating ideas in looksmaxxing forums; nutrition reviews generally have not supported the harm claims.

chain: Calorie intake and body fat fall
fasting-for-face-fat.text: Users adopt intermittent fasting such as time-restricted eating or 5:2 to lower body fat and slim the face as part of cutting and hollow-cheek aesthetics. Trials show weight loss comparable to ordinary calorie reduction; facial fat has not been tested specifically.

extreme-dieting-low-body-fat.text: Called leanmaxxing, this means cutting to roughly 10 to 15% body fat for facial definition and visible muscle. Forum members disagree on the ideal level and note that facial fat distribution is partly genetic. Sports medicine documents the practice in competition prep.

tapeworm-diet.text: The tapeworm diet is an old fad-diet story in which swallowing a tapeworm is meant to produce weight loss and a leaner look. Wikipedia describes it among 19th-century diet hoaxes; medical sources describe infection as a disease, and no appearance studies exist.

cold-showers.text: Users take cold showers for claimed benefits to skin, hair, testosterone, mood and discipline. Meta-analyses find mood and stress effects of uncertain strength; the skin, hair and hormone claims are based on anecdote.

cold-plunge-face-ice-dunk.text: Looksmaxxing users dunk the face in ice water mainly to reduce morning puffiness and tighten the look of the skin. Whole-body cold plunges are linked more to recovery. The facial routine is popular on forums, with no published trials on it.

sungazing.text: Some users sungaze in the hope of lightening iris color or improving vision. The practice dates to early 20th-century eye exercises. The iris-lightening idea rests on belief and anecdote, and ophthalmology literature documents retinal burns from it.

urine-therapy.text: Followers of urine therapy drink or apply urine, sometimes aged, for rejuvenation and skin. The practice has roots in yoga traditions. The appearance claims rest on tradition and anecdote, with no studies showing a benefit.

sunbathing-tanmaxxing.text: Tanmaxxing means darkening the skin with sun, lamps, tanning lotions or sunless products for a healthier, more attractive complexion. The color change is immediately visible. Tanning is the skin's pigment response to ultraviolet radiation.

sleepmaxxing.text: Users optimise sleep with darkness, routines, blue-light blocking and sometimes supplements or peptides, aiming for brighter skin, fewer dark circles and better recovery. Sleep hygiene has weak-to-mixed trial support for insomnia; effects on looks specifically are untested.

smellmaxxing.text: Smellmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for managing body scent with hygiene, deodorant and fragrance as part of overall attractiveness. It is a minor topic. Body-odour science exists, though there is little published on the looksmaxxing claims.

gymmaxxing.text: Gymmaxxing is lifting and leaning out for looks, usually emphasising leanness and shoulder width. Muscle-building physiology is well described; the effect on attractiveness specifically is untested. Some forum members argue lifting cannot offset facial flaws.

alcohol-sugar-dairy-face-avoidance.text: Users drop alcohol, added sugar and dairy hoping for a less puffy, clearer, leaner face. Related acne and hydration research exists; facial leanness itself has not been tested for these changes.

softmaxxing.text: Softmaxxing is the non-invasive end of looksmaxxing: skincare, haircuts, grooming, clothing, posture and weight management. Forum guides describe it as low-risk and reversible. The label itself has not been tested, though many component habits are visibly effective.

body-dysmorphia-mirror-checking.text: Body dysmorphic disorder and mirror checking come up in looksmaxxing communities as the mental-health side of appearance focus. It is a recognised psychiatric condition marked by preoccupation with minor perceived flaws, which clinicians treat with CBT and SSRIs.

subliminals-for-appearance.text: Listeners play subliminal audio hoping to grow taller, change eye color, improve jaw growth or reduce hair loss through the subconscious. No study has tested physical change from these recordings, and forum members are themselves split, with some attributing effects to expectation.

colloidal-silver.text: Colloidal silver is promoted in alternative-health circles as a supplement and immune aid, and appears in appearance forums in eye color discussions. Wikipedia states no medical evidence supports the health claims; chronic use can cause blue-grey skin (argyria).

eye-color-change-drops.text: Users discuss drops, such as latanoprost-type or homemade ones, to lighten brown eyes toward blue, green or hazel, alongside keratopigmentation and laser depigmentation. No peer-reviewed study has examined a cosmetic drop for this; surgical routes carry documented eye risks.
